title: Last Lunch

jokes.text: Opening scene: Liz Lemon wrangling kids named 'Janet' and 'Criss' — then telling her husband Criss 'shoes and socks' like a third child
jokes.setup: Liz is ordering her kids around in a chaotic morning rush
jokes.punchline: She then has to tell her adult husband Criss the same thing — 'Criss, shoes and socks!' — treating him like one of the children
jokes.explanation: Efficient character establishment — Liz's controlling, parental energy extends naturally to her husband. Good economy, works as character comedy.

jokes.text: Internet comment thread: 'Is that like a girl doctor? Go back to Saudi Arabia, Hitler!'
jokes.setup: Someone innocently asks for a recommendation for a girl's bike on the Upper West Side
jokes.punchline: A commenter responds by questioning what a 'girl's bike' is, comparing it to a 'girl doctor,' then immediately leaping to 'Go back to Saudi Arabia, Hitler!'
jokes.explanation: Brilliant satirical compression of internet comment culture — the escalation from mild confusion to 'Hitler!' is perfectly calibrated. The absurdist leap is funny because it's so recognizably accurate. Strong originality and economy.

jokes.text: 'Helmets inhibit brain development. You might as well give your darling child vaccines, which studies show cause homosexuality.'
jokes.setup: A commenter criticizes not buying a helmet for the bike
jokes.punchline: Another commenter counters that helmets inhibit brain development and pivots to vaccines causing homosexuality — escalating anti-vax paranoia to absurdist extremes
jokes.explanation: Excellent satirical escalation — the 'vaccines cause homosexuality' twist is a sharp satirical jab at anti-vax conspiracy logic. The non-sequitur conclusion is perfectly absurd.

jokes.text: 'So what? My two-year-old is super gay, and we love him more than a straight child because he doesn't rape!'
jokes.setup: Commenter says vaccines cause homosexuality
jokes.punchline: The retort doubles down with 'we love him more than a straight child because he doesn't rape' — a wildly dark non-sequitur that satirizes performative progressive parenting
jokes.explanation: Peak 30 Rock internet satire — the punchline is so shockingly dark and compressed that it becomes hilarious. 'Because he doesn't rape' as a parenting credential is a genuinely original absurdist construction. One of the episode's best individual lines.

jokes.text: Jack reveals he moved Kabletown's customer service to 'a part of India that has no phones' — providing the same service at zero cost
jokes.setup: Jack is presenting corporate achievements to his board
jokes.punchline: He moved customer service to a part of India with no phones — the absurdist logic delivered with complete corporate sincerity
jokes.explanation: Classic Jack Donaghy corporate absurdism. The joke is perfectly character-integrated — only Jack would present this as a triumph. The logic is airtight in its absurdity.

jokes.text: The Six Sigma 'wheel of domination' is replacing Kabletown's 'kitten in spaghetti' motivational poster
jokes.setup: Jack introduces a corporate motivational tool
jokes.punchline: He mentions it will replace Kabletown's existing motivational tool — 'kitten in spaghetti' — a perfectly idiotic corporate image that lands as a throwaway
jokes.explanation: The phrase 'kitten in spaghetti' is a perfect throwaway — specific enough to be funny, absurd enough to satirize corporate culture. Good economy.

jokes.text: 'And then we'll be able to get even better trophy wives... Half-Asian ones!'
jokes.setup: Jack says once the wheel is complete, they'll be a perfect company
jokes.punchline: A board member adds that they'll then be able to get better trophy wives — 'half-Asian ones' — satire of corporate elite entitlement
jokes.explanation: Competent satire of the boardroom's grotesque priorities, though it leans a bit cheap on the racial punchline. Works in context but not memorable.

jokes.text: Liz reveals she caught Jonathan (Jack's assistant) in a wedding dress, dancing with one of Jack's suits late at night
jokes.setup: Jonathan tries to stop Liz from entering Jack's office
jokes.punchline: Liz reveals she once came up late at night and found Jonathan in a wedding dress dancing with one of Jack's suits — Jonathan immediately stands down
jokes.explanation: Exceptional character joke — Jonathan's obsessive devotion to Jack has been a running gag, and this takes it to a perfectly surreal conclusion. The specificity (wedding dress, dancing with a suit) is inspired. The instant capitulation is the perfect button. Justifies 8+ for character integration and originality.

jokes.text: Jonathan immediately says 'Mr. Donaghy will see you now' after Liz's wedding dress revelation
jokes.setup: Liz has just exposed Jonathan's secret
jokes.punchline: Jonathan's only response is to instantly capitulate with robotic professionalism, neither confirming nor denying the wedding dress story
jokes.explanation: The comedic timing of the instant pivot to professional mode is perfect. Jonathan saying nothing and simply opening the door is funnier than any denial or explanation could be. Economy score is near-perfect — the joke is entirely in what's NOT said.

jokes.text: 'Stay-at-home Lemon. To what do I owe the pleasure? Did you already run out of things to do today?'
jokes.setup: Liz shows up at Jack's office
jokes.punchline: Jack immediately sees through her — she's only been a stay-at-home mom for presumably days and has already run out of things to do
jokes.explanation: Solid character beat — Jack's incisive reading of Liz is perfectly in-character. 'Stay-at-home Lemon' as a greeting is a nice economy.

jokes.text: 'I ran this morning for 30 minutes.' 'Does that include dry heaving?' 'And wet.'
jokes.setup: Liz insists she has plenty of new outlets including a morning run
jokes.punchline: Jack asks if that includes dry heaving; Liz confirms 'and wet' — doubling down on her own physical incompetence
jokes.explanation: Three-word punchline ('And wet.') that perfectly encapsulates Liz's physical ineptitude. Structure is very clean — setup, zinger, button. The 'wet heaving' detail is the right level of gross for maximum comedy.

jokes.text: Criss has a degree in ethno-musicology from Wesleyan, so he's a receptionist in a dental office
jokes.setup: Liz explains Criss has gone back to work
jokes.punchline: His degree is in ethno-musicology from Wesleyan — so naturally he's a dental receptionist
jokes.explanation: Sharp observational joke about liberal arts degrees and underemployment. The specificity of 'ethno-musicology from Wesleyan' is doing real comedic work — it's funnier than a generic arts degree.

jokes.text: 'Hogcock! Which is a combination of hogwash and poppycock.'
jokes.setup: Liz says Jack is the emotionally fragile one
jokes.punchline: Jack dismisses her with 'Hogcock!' — then explains it's a portmanteau of hogwash and poppycock
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's most quotable single-word jokes. The word 'hogcock' is inherently funny — it sounds obscene while meaning nothing of the sort. The explanation adds a secondary laugh. Perfectly Jack Donaghy: pompous, verbose, yet somehow efficient. Justifies 8+ for originality, economy, and quotability.

jokes.text: Jack's speech about being a god looking down from his office window, watching 'the swinish multitude,' the 'beard-havers and bicycle riders'
jokes.setup: Jack shows Liz his view and delivers a grandiose speech about his power
jokes.punchline: The speech climaxes with him including 'beard-havers and bicycle riders' among his ideological enemies — then declaring himself a god
jokes.explanation: 'Beard-havers and bicycle riders' as political enemies is a perfect satirical compression of conservative paranoia. The escalation to declaring himself 'a god' and Liz's flat 'And this makes you happy?' — 'It should.' is a beautiful button.

jokes.text: 'And this makes you happy?' 'It should.'
jokes.setup: Jack delivers his god-of-capitalism speech
jokes.punchline: Liz asks if this makes him happy; Jack answers 'It should' — revealing his entire worldview is built on what he thinks happiness ought to be rather than what it is
jokes.explanation: Two words ('It should') that perfectly encapsulate the entire series' thesis about Jack Donaghy. Maximum economy — it's both funny and genuinely revealing. The gap between what Jack thinks should make him happy and what does is the engine of his character arc. One of the episode's best crafted moments.

jokes.text: Liz doing a Yoda impression — 'Mmm! Ohh! Dark times are these.'
jokes.setup: Liz says she is reminded of something Yoda once said
jokes.punchline: She delivers a bizarrely committed Yoda impression — 'Mmm! Ohh! Dark times are these' — as genuine emotional wisdom
jokes.explanation: Perfectly Liz Lemon — she deploys Star Wars wisdom sincerely in a moment of genuine emotional conversation. Works because of character integration.

jokes.text: Japanese game show contestants could win money 'instead of penis punches'
jokes.setup: NBC wants to adapt a Japanese game show for American audiences
jokes.punchline: The polite suggestion that contestants could win money 'instead of penis punches' — delivered as a diplomatic note
jokes.explanation: The phrase 'penis punches' delivered in a corporate diplomatic register is the joke. The juxtaposition of polite business language with extreme physical comedy is sharp.

jokes.text: 'And yet you still say stupid stuff to me all the time and suck at carrying boxes!'
jokes.setup: Tracy is told that sometimes things change when people get promoted
jokes.punchline: Tracy points out that Dotcom and Grizz still do useless things for him — which means he still deserves Kenneth's service too
jokes.explanation: Tracy's logic is impeccably absurd — he's arguing for Kenneth's subservience by citing that his other friends are also subservient and useless. Very character-specific.

jokes.text: Kenneth offers Liz 'chickpeas, moonshine, turtle meat' as refreshments
jokes.setup: Kenneth, now network president, asks if he can get Liz anything
jokes.punchline: His offerings are 'chickpeas, moonshine, turtle meat' — rural Southern poverty foods delivered in a presidential register
jokes.explanation: Perfect character joke — Kenneth has become NBC president but still thinks in terms of Stone Mountain, Georgia subsistence living. 'Turtle meat' as the third item after chickpeas and moonshine is an inspired escalation. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: Kenneth's list of TV no-no words includes 'woman, writer, New York' and he wants shows where 'a guy gets a drink thrown in his face and turns to his dog and says don't even say it'
jokes.setup: Liz pitches a show about a woman writer living in New York
jokes.punchline: Kenneth says 'woman, writer, New York' are all TV no-no words — then describes the ideal show as a man getting a drink thrown at him, turning to his dog who says nothing because it's a dog
jokes.explanation: Exceptional meta-comedy — 30 Rock is literally the show Kenneth is saying doesn't work. The dog-drink bit is a perfect parody of empty network comedy logic. 'Don't even say it' to a dog is such a specific, perfectly stupid image. One of the episode's strongest jokes. Justifies 8+ for originality, structure, and self-referential audacity.

jokes.text: Kenneth makes the face Liz just described while referencing quality TV, and Liz makes it too
jokes.setup: Kenneth says audiences don't want 'angry New York crankypants making that face'
jokes.punchline: Liz involuntarily makes exactly that face as she absorbs the criticism
jokes.explanation: A strong visual gag that works through self-fulfillment — Liz proving Kenneth's point by making the exact face he's describing. The humor is in the instant self-awareness and the absence of denial. A physical comedy moment elevated by its meta quality.

jokes.text: Jenna threatens to 'tell the other gays your real ages' to her makeup team
jokes.setup: Jenna throws a tantrum in the makeup room demanding her color
jokes.punchline: Her escalating threats include threatening to reveal the makeup artists' real ages to 'the other gays'
jokes.explanation: Classic Jenna — her weapons are always so specifically showbiz and petty. The age-revealing threat to the gay makeup community is perfectly calibrated to her character.

jokes.text: 'How dare you, you rotting pear? I will stop being an actress when the earth stops spinning on Kabbalah monster's fingernail.'
jokes.setup: A crew member points out Jenna is technically not an actor anymore since the show is over
jokes.punchline: Jenna responds with the insult 'rotting pear' and the declaration she'll stop acting 'when the earth stops spinning on Kabbalah monster's fingernail'
jokes.explanation: 'Kabbalah monster's fingernail' is a brilliantly bizarre construction — it's an insane cosmic image that somehow perfectly captures celebrity spirituality delusion. 'Rotting pear' as an insult is inspired. Quintessential Jenna in peak form. Justifies 8+ for originality and character integration.

jokes.text: 'Good-bye forever, you factory reject dildos.'
jokes.setup: Jenna declares she's done with the show and only does dramatic roles now
jokes.punchline: Her grand exit line is 'Good-bye forever, you factory reject dildos' — then she exits
jokes.explanation: 'Factory reject dildos' is an extremely specific and hilarious insult — it's not just obscene, it implies defects. Perfectly Jenna. Very high quotability. The 'good-bye forever' setup makes it land harder.

jokes.text: Jack to Inga: 'I'm afraid I'm gonna have to spank you again.'
jokes.setup: Jack is annoyed that Inga didn't warn him about an important guest arriving
jokes.punchline: 'I'm afraid I'm gonna have to spank you again' — delivered as routine workplace discipline, with the 'again' implying this is established practice
jokes.explanation: The 'again' does the heavy lifting — it implies an established pattern. Competent joke, though the spanking-boss formula is familiar territory.

jokes.text: Kenneth: 'Where are all the baby pigeons?' in response to Jack saying he's been thinking about happiness
jokes.setup: Jack says he's been thinking about something that's never bothered him until now
jokes.punchline: Kenneth, thinking they're comparing notes, jumps in with 'Where are all the baby pigeons?' — completely missing Jack's emotional register
jokes.explanation: Brilliant Kenneth joke — his oblivious literalism is perfectly calibrated. 'Where are all the baby pigeons?' is a genuine philosophical question that makes perfect absurdist sense coming from Kenneth. The mismatch between Jack's existential vulnerability and Kenneth's pigeon concern is perfectly timed. Justifies 8+ for originality, structure, and character integration.

jokes.text: Kenneth's pig analogy: 'If a pig says, can I communicate with you telepathically, do I have a soul? And you're like, no. Duh. Into the slaughtering chute.'
jokes.setup: Jack asks if not feeling happy means he has a problem
jokes.punchline: Kenneth offers the wisdom that if you have to ask if you're happy, you're not — illustrated by a pig asking if it has a soul and being sent to slaughter
jokes.explanation: Exceptional Kenneth wisdom — he delivers a genuinely profound philosophical point via a horrifying pig slaughter metaphor. The specificity of 'into the slaughtering chute' after the almost tender pig-communicating-telepathically setup is a perfect comedic pivot. Very strong originality.

jokes.text: The Six Sigma acronym: Analyze, Strategize, Succeed — 'A.S.S.' — 'I'm going to crush this problem with my ass.'
jokes.setup: Jack says every problem can be solved using Six Sigma: Analyze, Strategize, Succeed
jokes.punchline: He spells out the acronym — A.S.S. — then declares 'I'm going to crush this problem with my ass'
jokes.explanation: The acronym is a setup_punchline gem — the reveal of A.S.S. is telegraphed but the character-specific button 'I'm going to crush this problem with my ass,' delivered with Jack's total sincerity, makes it land hard. The corporate-language framework sells it completely.

jokes.text: Tracy spells out his name for the receptionist: 'T as in the drink, R as in the pirate noise, A as in the Fonzie noise, C as in sea monster, Y as in why do we even make friends if they're gonna let you down when we need them most?'
jokes.setup: Tracy arrives at Kenneth's office and is told he's in a meeting — Tracy leaves his name
jokes.punchline: Tracy's phonetic alphabet includes 'T as in the drink,' 'R as in the pirate noise,' 'A as in the Fonzie noise,' and then the Y becomes an extended emotional breakdown — 'why do we even make friends if they're gonna let you down when we need them most?'
jokes.explanation: One of the greatest Tracy Jordan moments in the series. The escalating absurdity of each letter (pirate noise, Fonzie noise, sea monster) builds perfectly to the emotional gut-punch of 'Y as in why do we even make friends...' — which is both hilarious and genuinely touching. The structural conceit of a phonetic alphabet becoming a cry for help is inspired. The joke earns its emotional resonance. Clearly the strongest single joke construction in the episode.

jokes.text: Mom forum: 'I put all my old work energy into parenting. My kids hate me, which gives me more parenting to do.'
jokes.setup: A stay-at-home mom offers advice on channeling work energy into parenting
jokes.punchline: Her kids hate her, which just creates more parenting to do — a perfectly circular and bleak logic
jokes.explanation: Beautifully bleak. The circular logic of 'my kids hate me so now I have more parenting to do' is darkly funny and economically perfect.

jokes.text: Forum reply: 'I did [switch places with stay-at-home moms], but I got fired... For stupidity.'
jokes.setup: A working parent says they'd switch places with stay-at-home moms
jokes.punchline: 'I did, but I got fired... for stupidity.' — the ellipsis and specificity of 'stupidity' make it land
jokes.explanation: The beat before 'for stupidity' is the key — the pause implies something shameful, then 'stupidity' is both specific and universal. Nice economy.

jokes.text: Forum poster: 'I'd switch places with any of you. And I have amazing cheekbones.'
jokes.setup: The forum debate about working vs. stay-at-home parenting
jokes.punchline: A poster adds 'I'd switch places with any of you. And I have amazing cheekbones.' — the cheekbones detail is completely irrelevant and reveals character
jokes.explanation: A perfect throwaway — the cheekbones claim has nothing to do with the argument and reveals that this is actually Liz, bragging anonymously online. Later pays off when Criss recognizes the detail.

jokes.text: T.I. quote paraphrased as 'better get on yo job, tell 'em. Haters get on yo job, nougats' — 'at least I think he was saying nougats'
jokes.setup: A poster claims work can be fulfilling, citing rapper T.I.
jokes.punchline: The T.I. lyric is misquoted with 'nougats' replacing an obvious profanity, followed by the earnest parenthetical 'at least I think he was saying nougats'
jokes.explanation: A nice layered joke — the misquote reveals the poster's demographic (white, doesn't listen to T.I. much), and 'nougats' is a perfect candy-bar substitute for the obvious word. The sincere caveat makes it funnier.

jokes.text: The forum fight concludes with one poster planning to attack the other at 'hippo playground' — 'I'll be the one wearing a purple sweater and wrapping a baby swing around some skank's neck'
jokes.setup: The mom forum argument escalates from advice to personal attacks
jokes.punchline: One poster arranges an actual physical fight at the hippo playground, describing herself by her sweater and her intent to weaponize baby equipment
jokes.explanation: The internet-argument-to-real-world-violence escalation is perfectly executed. 'Wrapping a baby swing around some skank's neck' is darkly specific and very funny. The mundane 'purple sweater' detail grounds it perfectly.

jokes.text: Jack's 'ass attack' karate fight sequence where he defeats a much younger man and declares 'Now I am the sensei! The parking space closest to the door is mine.'
jokes.setup: Jack says he is going to 'crush this problem with my ass' using Six Sigma
jokes.punchline: Cut to Jack in a parking garage apparently winning a karate fight, screaming 'Now I am the sensei! The parking space closest to the door is mine!'
jokes.explanation: Absurdist cutaway that pays off the A.S.S. joke. The specific prize — the closest parking space — perfectly deflates the grandiosity. Jack winning a physical altercation over a parking spot as a solution to his existential unhappiness is surreal.

jokes.text: The Colonel as weather co-host advises viewers to 'get hit by a car' to get free hospital soup
jokes.setup: A TV weather segment with a co-host called 'the Colonel'
jokes.punchline: The Colonel's winter advice: 'if you can, get hit by a car. You get to spend a couple days in the hospital, and they'll give you soup.'
jokes.explanation: Beautifully dark homeless-person logic delivered in a cheery weather-broadcast register. The soup motivation is a perfect specific detail — not warmth, not shelter, but soup.

jokes.text: Jack's fantasy: 'Nancy, I know this is unconventional, but I think a group relationship could work.' / 'What you're proposing is a sin, Jack, but she is wicked hot.' / 'It would have to be a conjugal visit because I am in a Puerto Rican jail.'
jokes.setup: Jack's fantasy/daydream of potential happiness involves his two ex-loves
jokes.punchline: The fantasy includes Nancy's Boston Catholicism ('it's a sin, but she is wicked hot') and Elisa revealing she's in a Puerto Rican jail — which apparently doesn't stop the fantasy
jokes.explanation: Callbacks to both Nancy (Boston Catholic) and Elisa (Puerto Rican murderer) are well-executed. 'Puerto Rican jail' is the perfect Elisa-specific punchline. The conjugal visit logistics becoming a plot point in a fantasy is very funny.

jokes.text: Jenna on Law & Order: 'I'm glad to finally return to my two loves... Dramatic acting and sex crimes.'
jokes.setup: Jenna is thrilled to be working on Law & Order
jokes.punchline: Her 'two loves' are dramatic acting and sex crimes — the specific enthusiasm for sex crimes is perfectly Jenna
jokes.explanation: The rhythm of the line is perfect — 'dramatic acting AND sex crimes.' The enthusiasm for sex crimes as a love interest is quintessentially Jenna. High quotability and strong character integration.

jokes.text: Jenna complains she dies in the L&O episode and asks how she'll become a recurring character — then how she'll 'get away with horrible stuff, like this'
jokes.setup: Jenna discovers her character dies in the first scene
jokes.punchline: Her concern is not dramatic — she's worried about becoming recurring, and specifically about getting away with 'horrible stuff, like this' — whatever she then does that we don't see
jokes.explanation: Classic Jenna self-interest — her entire concern is career advancement and impunity, not the work itself. 'Horrible stuff, like this' followed by an implied visual gag is a nice construction.

jokes.text: Jenna filming L&O: found 'dead,' then says 'Oh, still alive.' Then: 'Ow! My foot hurts, but I'm okay. I think this injury has given me crime-solving powers. It's Law & Order: Mind Beauty.'
jokes.setup: Law & Order detectives find Jenna's 'body' — she's supposed to be dead
jokes.punchline: Jenna speaks ('Oh, still alive'), injures herself, then invents a spinoff — 'Law & Order: Mind Beauty' — based on her foot injury giving her crime-solving powers
jokes.explanation: 'Law & Order: Mind Beauty' is a perfectly stupid fake spinoff name — it sounds like a real L&O spinoff title (compare 'SVU,' 'Criminal Intent') but means absolutely nothing. The leap from foot injury to crime-solving powers is flawlessly absurd Jenna logic.

jokes.text: Jenna's farewell insult from the Law & Order set: 'Good-bye forever, you soup line at a gay homeless shelter.'
jokes.setup: Jenna storms off the set
jokes.punchline: 'Soup line at a gay homeless shelter' — another of Jenna's impossibly specific exit insults
jokes.explanation: Part of Jenna's running gag of insane exit insults throughout the episode. 'Soup line at a gay homeless shelter' is even more specific and absurd than 'factory reject dildos' — it's simultaneously insulting (a line, a place of desperation) and weirdly specific (gay homeless shelter). The escalating specificity of Jenna's insults across the episode is one of its great running gags.

jokes.text: Criss at the park to fight: 'Liz, you don't want to be here right now, 'cause I got to go smack that woman in the face.' — it's Liz
jokes.setup: Criss arrives at the park playground, intent on fighting 'the original poster'
jokes.punchline: The original poster is Liz — his wife — and the reveal comes when she says 'You're here to fight me. I'm the original poster.'
jokes.explanation: Well-constructed payoff of the mom forum setup — the reveal is earned by the cheekbones clue planted earlier. Criss arriving ready to fight his own wife is a great image.

jokes.text: 'Oh, my god! Since when do you listen to T.I.?' / 'That message board is for moms. I thought you were a lady. You said you had amazing cheekbones.'
jokes.setup: Criss and Liz both realize they were arguing with each other on the forum
jokes.punchline: Criss's primary outrage is that the board is for moms and he thought he was arguing with a woman — and he was fooled by the cheekbones claim
jokes.explanation: Good callback payoff — 'I thought you were a lady' is funny because he's married to her. The cheekbones callback lands well.

jokes.text: Criss explains he hates work: keeps getting up for coffee and is now 'all jittery and weird and... bird!'
jokes.setup: Criss admits he hates the desk job at the dental office
jokes.punchline: He trails off mid-sentence, distracted by a bird — 'all jittery and weird and... BIRD!' — the coffee jitters have made him attention-span-free
jokes.explanation: The '...bird!' mid-sentence is a great comedic construction — it enacts the very thing he's describing (being distracted and jittery). Perfect economy and structural elegance.

jokes.text: 'Or that one where your hands are spiders.' 'Hand spiders.'
jokes.setup: Criss describes playing 'waiting games' like 'carpet adventure' with kids
jokes.punchline: Liz knows the game — 'hand spiders' — and they bond over it
jokes.explanation: Charming character moment — both Liz and Criss are playful nerds at heart. 'Hand spiders' as a game title is specific and delightful. Works as a warm comedic beat in an otherwise rapid-fire episode.

jokes.text: 'Oh, my god, if you were a dude, you would not even be thinking that [that you're a terrible mother for wanting to work].'
jokes.setup: Liz says she's a terrible mother for missing work
jokes.punchline: Criss points out that if she were a man, the double standard would mean she'd feel nothing — before concluding 'You're the dad.'
jokes.explanation: Solid observational point with a funny payoff ('You're the dad') — the gender role reversal is well-handled. Not especially original but well-executed.

jokes.text: 'I do like ignoring your questions while I try to watch TV.'
jokes.setup: Criss tells Liz she's 'the dad' in their relationship
jokes.punchline: Liz immediately and happily concedes this: 'I do like ignoring your questions while I try to watch TV.'
jokes.explanation: Perfect character line — Liz owning this dad-behavior with zero shame, even enthusiasm, is very funny. The specificity of 'ignoring your questions while I try to watch TV' is exactly right for her character.

jokes.text: Criss suggests Liz pitch a show about 'a dentist's office where the sassy hygienist says things like I'm turning 30... Again.' 'I will miss Tyrell.'
jokes.setup: Criss suggests Liz pitch a show to Kenneth
jokes.punchline: He describes a generic terrible sitcom — 'a sassy hygienist saying I'm turning 30... Again' — and then adds 'I will miss Tyrell,' mourning a character from his hypothetical terrible show
jokes.explanation: 'I will miss Tyrell' is a perfect button — Criss has already emotionally attached to the fake character from his hypothetical bad show. Meta and well-structured.

jokes.text: Tracy: 'I saw his schedule on his assistant's pornography box!' / Dotcom: 'You mean computer?'
jokes.setup: Tracy claims he saw Kenneth's schedule
jokes.punchline: Tracy calls the computer a 'pornography box' — Dotcom gently corrects him
jokes.explanation: 'Pornography box' for 'computer' is a perfectly Tracy neologism — simultaneously revealing his worldview and his disconnect from ordinary language. Dotcom's patience is the ideal straight-man response.

jokes.text: 'What am I? My son's piano recital?' — Tracy comparing being avoided to being skipped
jokes.setup: Tracy realizes Kenneth is avoiding him and not showing up
jokes.punchline: Tracy asks 'What am I? My son's piano recital?' — comparing himself to something he routinely skips
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best one-liners. The self-awareness is perfect — Tracy understands he's being treated like something he himself ignores. The piano recital specificity is inspired. Excellent economy and character integration.

jokes.text: 'Put yourself in Kenneth's shoes.' / 'I can't! He's not here! Stop torturing me!'
jokes.setup: Dotcom tries to reason with Tracy by asking him to empathize with Kenneth
jokes.punchline: Tracy takes 'put yourself in Kenneth's shoes' literally — he can't because Kenneth isn't present to supply the shoes
jokes.explanation: Classic Tracy literalism — the idiom parsed as a physical request. 'Stop torturing me!' elevates it perfectly. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: 'Unless you need us to hate the new Taylor Swift album. That girl has feelings.'
jokes.setup: Dotcom says they can do whatever Tracy needs except certain things
jokes.punchline: The exception is hating the Taylor Swift album — 'that girl has feelings'
jokes.explanation: Deadpan Dotcom observation — the joke is both a defense of Taylor Swift and a gentle mockery of her emotional reputation. Works as a quick aside.

jokes.text: Jack's solution to his happiness problem: talking two Catholic beauties into a 'vanilla-caramel sex swirl' and porking 'in that prison basement'
jokes.setup: Kenneth asks if Jack has figured out his happiness problem
jokes.punchline: Jack reveals he orchestrated a threesome with his two ex-loves — one of whom is currently in a Puerto Rican prison — and had sex in the prison basement, which was 'wicked awesome'
jokes.explanation: Payoff of the fantasy sequence — the absurdity is that Jack actually followed through. 'Vanilla-caramel sex swirl' is an inspired euphemism. Nancy's Boston accent infecting Jack ('wicked awesome') is a great detail.

jokes.text: Jack's fantasy sex swirl with Nancy and Elisa: 'Oh, Jack, porking in that prison basement was wicked awesome.'
jokes.setup: Jack describes achieving a fantasy with his two ex-girlfriends after various logistics
jokes.punchline: Nancy's enthusiastic review — 'porking in that prison basement was wicked awesome' — combining her Boston accent/slang with the prison setting
jokes.explanation: Good payoff to the fantasy setup. 'Wicked awesome' as Boston-Nancy's review combined with the logistics of a prison basement is good character-specific absurdism. The combination of the mundane ('porking') with the insane setting works.

jokes.text: Democratic congressman: 'If the Democratic party controlled Congress, I would see to it that he was punished in the worst way possible... By having to come down here and listen to us.'
jokes.setup: Jack is told Democrats don't know what to do with themselves over his salary
jokes.punchline: A congressman threatens the worst punishment possible — having to listen to Democratic senators talk
jokes.explanation: Good bipartisan self-deprecating joke — the Democrats are satirizing themselves as toothless and boring. The structure (threatening the worst punishment / which is their own company) is clean.

jokes.text: 'God, I feel like I have a macropenis right now.'
jokes.setup: Jack watches his enemies rage impotently about his wealth
jokes.punchline: His expression of satisfaction is 'I feel like I have a macropenis right now' — anatomical grandiosity as a power metaphor
jokes.explanation: 'Macropenis' (rather than a common vulgarity) is perfectly Jack — overly clinical yet obscene. His choice of vocabulary even for his own braggart moments is character-specific.

jokes.text: 'John Hardly. He loves his family but hates the rat race. He's hardly working.' — Liz pitching a show
jokes.setup: Kenneth said America doesn't want shows about Liz-type characters; Liz says he was right and pivots
jokes.punchline: Her new pitch: 'John Hardly' — a man who's 'hardly working.' The wordplay is the entire concept.
jokes.explanation: The pun is obvious but that's the joke — Liz is pitching a terrible concept. The meta layer (this is what NBC wants) saves it from being just a bad pun.

jokes.text: Kenneth mentions 'two Santas I saw kissing on the subway' while saying 'unusual clauses'
jokes.setup: Kenneth mentions Tracy's contract contains 'unusual clauses'
jokes.punchline: He clarifies he doesn't mean 'those two Santas I saw kissing on the subway' — a perfect phonetic pun on 'Clauses'/'Clauses'
jokes.explanation: Clauses/Claus pun is well-executed — the clarification is funnier than a straight pun because Kenneth volunteers the image of two Santas kissing. The specificity of subway adds a nice NYC detail.

jokes.text: 'Wow. You've really changed, Kenneth.' / 'I don't think so. You look nice today.' / 'Shut your chin slit.' / 'Yes, ma'am.'
jokes.setup: Kenneth uses his presidential authority to compel Liz to do one more episode of TGS
jokes.punchline: Liz says he's changed; Kenneth sincerely compliments her appearance; she tells him to 'shut your chin slit' — calling his dimple a slit — and he meekly agrees
jokes.explanation: 'Shut your chin slit' is a great insult — specific to Kenneth's chin dimple, and oddly anatomical. His instant 'Yes, ma'am' shows he hasn't changed at all despite being president. Strong character work.

jokes.text: Jenna at the LA airport, confronted by a wheelchair attendant — 'Shut it down.' — then announces she's returning to Broadway
jokes.setup: Jenna left for LA, having declared she's done with the show forever
jokes.punchline: She's been at the airport long enough to get offered a wheelchair — she responds 'Shut it down,' then immediately announces another new plan (Broadway)
jokes.explanation: Part of the running gag of Jenna's impossible exits — each goodbye is immediately followed by a new one. The wheelchair detail implies she's been at the airport a while but going nowhere.

jokes.text: Jenna's LAX exit insult: 'I will return to my first love... Broadway! You eastern European knockoff Mr. Potato Heads.'
jokes.setup: Jenna dramatically announces a new direction
jokes.punchline: 'Eastern European knockoff Mr. Potato Heads' as the LA crowd insult
jokes.explanation: The best of Jenna's exit insults in this episode. 'Eastern European knockoff Mr. Potato Heads' is an extraordinary combination of specificity — the Eastern European quality (suggesting cheap imitation), knockoff status, and the Mr. Potato Head imagery creating a vivid absurdist insult. The escalating specificity of Jenna's insults across the episode reaches its peak here. Fully justified high scores.

jokes.text: Tracy releases Kenneth from his promise, explaining he's 'not talking about my gout' when referencing blowing up overnight
jokes.setup: Tracy delivers an emotional speech about not wanting to be a burden to newly famous Kenneth
jokes.punchline: In the middle of the sincere speech he clarifies 'I'm not talking about my gout' — as if gout-based overnight blowing up is the first interpretation one would reach
jokes.explanation: Perfect Tracy move — the emotional moment is punctured by a medical aside, but the aside is so Tracy-specific (gout) that it enhances rather than deflates the emotion. The parenthetical structure is very well handled.

jokes.text: Tracy confronts Kenneth: 'I'm Tracy Jordan. I don't answer phones.'
jokes.setup: Kenneth says he tried to call Tracy but no one answered
jokes.punchline: Tracy corrects him — the issue isn't that he wasn't available, it's that he doesn't answer phones as a matter of identity
jokes.explanation: Perfect Tracy joke — short, character-specific, and funny as a statement of identity. 'I'm Tracy Jordan. I don't answer phones.' treats not answering phones as a defining character trait, which for Tracy it genuinely is. Extremely economical.

jokes.text: Tracy gives Kenneth a tissue — Kenneth wonders 'Am I supposed to drop this on the floor?' — then immediately pivots to 'my car ran out of gas on the long island expressway'
jokes.setup: Tracy hands Kenneth a tissue for his emotional moment
jokes.punchline: Kenneth's reaction to being moved is confusion about tissue disposal protocol — then he immediately pivots to needing gas money (or a favor)
jokes.explanation: Kenneth's social awkwardness about tissue disposal is good. The immediate pivot to a favor request undercuts the emotional moment in a funny way.

jokes.text: Tracy's follow-up after the emotional moment: 'And while we're naming things, my car ran out of gas on the Long Island Expressway.'
jokes.setup: Tracy has just delivered an emotionally generous speech to Kenneth
jokes.punchline: He immediately follows genuine emotion with a practical complaint about his car
jokes.explanation: Perfect comedic deflation after an emotional moment — Tracy's needs are immediate and practical. The LIE detail is specific enough to feel real. This is a classic sitcom rhythm executed with Tracy's character perfectly.

jokes.text: Liz to Jack: 'I'm looking for six figures, eight if you're counting cents, which I fell for once before... Not cool, The Gap.'
jokes.setup: Liz asks Jack for a job and states her salary requirements
jokes.punchline: 'Six figures, eight if you're counting cents, which I fell for once before... Not cool, The Gap.' — revealing she was previously tricked by a salary that was six figures in cents
jokes.explanation: This is exceptional. The joke has multiple layers: (1) the financial naivety of counting cents as part of figures, (2) the revelation that The Gap once exploited this exact naivety, (3) the complete specificity of naming The Gap as the villain. The ellipsis before 'Not cool, The Gap' is perfectly timed. This is Liz Lemon at her most specific and funniest — absolutely justified at 8.5.

jokes.text: Jack: 'I got the job. I pissed off my enemies — Pelosi, Maddow, Baldwin. It should have been the greatest moment of my life.'
jokes.setup: Jack explains why he resigned from Kabletown
jokes.punchline: His enemies list — Pelosi, Maddow, Baldwin — is characteristically specific Jack conservatism, and 'it should have been the greatest moment' echoes his earlier 'It should' about happiness
jokes.explanation: The enemies list is perfectly Jack. The callback to 'It should' adds thematic weight to what could have been a simple name-drop joke.

jokes.text: 'You're just an alcoholic with a great voice.'
jokes.setup: Liz accuses Jack of not knowing what he's talking about after years of dispensing advice
jokes.punchline: 'You're just an alcoholic with a great voice' — stripping Jack down to two accurate traits
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best lines. Maximum economy — six words that are both a devastating insult and weirdly affectionate. 'A great voice' as the one concession is the perfect specific detail (Alec Baldwin's voice is legendarily good). The juxtaposition of alcoholic with the single compliment is structurally perfect. Easily justifies 8+ for economy and structure.

jokes.text: Jack: 'You're just an alcoholic with a great voice.'
jokes.setup: Liz is confronting Jack about his advice being useless all along
jokes.punchline: 'An alcoholic with a great voice' — reduces his entire authority to two traits, one negative, one superficial
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best lines. Six words that perfectly summarize Jack Donaghy while being devastating. The 'great voice' softener makes it funnier than pure insult — she can't help acknowledging the voice. Maximum economy, perfect character integration.

jokes.text: 'Eating night cheese and transitioning my pajamas into daywear.'
jokes.setup: Liz says when Jack met her she was perfectly happy
jokes.punchline: Her pre-Jack contentment was defined by 'eating night cheese and transitioning my pajamas into daywear' — two perfect specific Liz behaviors
jokes.explanation: 'Night cheese' is one of the most iconic 30 Rock Liz Lemon phrases — it's specific, weird, and utterly recognizable. 'Transitioning my pajamas into daywear' is equally perfect. Together they're a masterclass in character-specific comedy writing. The joke is that this was genuinely her idea of happiness and she says it with zero irony. Absolutely earns 8.6.

jokes.text: 'So we ruined each other?'
jokes.setup: Jack and Liz have both argued that the other is responsible for their current state
jokes.punchline: Liz's clean summation — 'So we ruined each other?' — treated as a logical conclusion rather than a tragedy
jokes.explanation: Perfect Lemon deadpan. The joke is in the phrasing — she accepts the devastating conclusion as a perfectly reasonable thing to say, with neither drama nor grief, just casual acknowledgment. The economy is near-perfect.

jokes.text: 'I used to be a shark, and then you unsharkulated me.'
jokes.setup: Jack blames Liz for making him soft and emotional
jokes.punchline: 'You unsharkulated me' — Jack inventing corporate-speak jargon to describe being defanged
jokes.explanation: 'Unsharkulated' is a brilliant coinage — the '-ulated' suffix gives it a corporate/medical weight. Only Jack Donaghy would use a word like this to describe emotional vulnerability. It's funny and also reveals his character. Justifies 8+ for originality, economy, and character integration.

jokes.text: Jonathan enters Jack's office screaming 'There! You're no longer special to him! Get out! Get out of our lives! Yes!'
jokes.setup: Jack and Liz have their big argument and seem to be parting ways
jokes.punchline: Jonathan rushes in, pumping his fist, delighted that Liz is out of Jack's life — 'Get out of our lives!'
jokes.explanation: 'Get out of our lives!' is the key detail — Jonathan has fully merged his identity with Jack's. His joy is indecent and perfect. The celebration of what is an emotionally devastating moment for the main characters is a great comedic counterpoint. Justifies 8+ for character integration.

jokes.text: 'TGS has done 149 shows. So we're gonna need you to go ahead and do one more.' — Kenneth's corporate pivot revealed as a callback
jokes.setup: Kenneth reveals Tracy's contract requires 150 episodes or NBC pays him $30 million
jokes.punchline: TGS has done exactly 149 — one short — so they must do one more. This retroactively makes all of Kenneth's earlier encouragement a trap.
jokes.explanation: Good structural comedy — the 149 episodes revelation recontextualizes Kenneth's earlier conversation. The irony that Liz needs a job AND is contractually required to do this one is well-crafted.

jokes.text: The 'snowicane' weather forecast specifically targeting 'midtown Manhattan between Saks Fifth Avenue and the variety deli'
jokes.setup: A snowicane is coming; crew members start leaving
jokes.punchline: The weather warning is so specific it names the exact two-block radius of the NBC building — 'midtown Manhattan between Saks Fifth Avenue and the variety deli'
jokes.explanation: The hyper-specificity of the warning zone makes it clearly manufactured. 'The variety deli' as one of the landmarks is a perfect New York-specific absurdist detail.

jokes.text: Liz's description of holding Tracy down: 'like that machine Kathy Geiss invented that hugs old people.' Cut to: machine malfunctioning and hurting someone.
jokes.setup: Liz says she'll hold Tracy down 'like that machine Kathy Geiss invented that hugs old people'
jokes.punchline: Cut to Kathy Geiss's machine hugging an old person, then apparently malfunctioning ('Whoops. Nope.')
jokes.explanation: Strong cutaway visual gag. Kathy Geiss's elder-care hugging machine is already a funny concept — the benevolent but probably frightening technology. The cutaway that shows it malfunctioning ('My god, this will change elder care forever' / 'Whoops. Nope.') is perfectly timed dark comedy. The 'Whoops. Nope.' reaction beat is the key — it implies something terrible has happened with complete economy.

jokes.text: Jack's description of where he's been: 'I assume that's code for a billionaire's soul-searching trip to tan penis island.'
jokes.setup: Jack says he's going away for 'probably a long time'
jokes.punchline: Liz names his destination as 'tan penis island' — implying a real place billionaires go
jokes.explanation: Exceptional naming joke. 'Tan penis island' is a perfect absurdist proper noun — it sounds like a real place, implies exactly the kind of hedonistic billionaire retreat it would be, and is memorably vulgar without being gratuitous. The confidence with which Liz names it as a known destination elevates the joke.

jokes.text: The snowicane forecast also specifies: 'get in your purple Bentley and be home with your sharks before the tristate area gets slammed by snowicane white lady name like Dorva or something'
jokes.setup: The suspiciously specific weather forecast continues
jokes.punchline: The forecast instructs someone with a purple Bentley to get home to their sharks, and names the storm 'white lady name like Dorva or something' — clearly written by Tracy
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. Tracy has written a weather forecast so specific to himself that it's unmistakably his, yet it airs on TV. 'White lady name like Dorva or something' is genius — the uncertainty ('or something') while naming the storm is absurdly perfect. Justifies 8+ for originality, character integration, and structure.

jokes.text: Al Roker is coerced via a convoluted hospital charity gala threat — 'his wife is on the board of a children's hospital, and they need a celebrity to host their annual gala, and I threatened to do it'
jokes.setup: Liz asks what Jack did to Al Roker to make him deliver the fake forecast
jokes.punchline: Jack threatened to host a children's hospital gala — the implied horror being that Jack Donaghy hosting a children's charity event would be a catastrophe
jokes.explanation: The logic is perfectly inverted — threatening to do something charitable as leverage. Only Jack could weaponize charity. The specificity of 'children's hospital gala' is key.

jokes.text: Tracy: 'But I promised Barbra Streisand I'd never stab her again!'
jokes.setup: Liz is trying to get Tracy back to do the show and tells him to cut the BS
jokes.punchline: Tracy's excuse for not being able to go on stage is that he promised Barbra Streisand he'd never stab her again — an entirely new backstory delivered as a throwaway
jokes.explanation: Exceptional throwaway. 'I'd never stab her again' implies a complete history with Barbra Streisand that the show has never mentioned and will never explain. The 'again' is doing all the work — it confirms this has happened before. The non-sequitur logic as an excuse is pure Tracy. One of the episode's best individual lines.

jokes.text: Jenna sharing Jack's breakdown: 'Did Liz scream in your face? Did you pin her up against the wall? Were your shirts wet with rain?' — describing a romantic movie fight
jokes.setup: Jack tells Jenna he and Liz had an argument that felt different
jokes.punchline: Jenna's version of an argument sounds like a romantic movie — screaming, pinning against walls, wet shirts — she's framing it as passion, not conflict
jokes.explanation: Jenna's romantic interpretation of workplace conflict is perfectly her. 'Were your shirts wet with rain?' is a great specific movie-romantic detail.

jokes.text: Jenna: 'When Conan dumped her, she dropped him forever.' Cut to: Young Conan O'Brien trying to get Liz's attention. 'We were gonna lose our virginity to each other! Now I'll never lose it!'
jokes.setup: Jenna says Liz never stays friends with exes and once dated Conan O'Brien
jokes.punchline: Cut to young Conan pleading with Liz that they were going to lose their virginity together — 'Now I'll never lose it!' — which is both sad and an absurd implication about Conan's life
jokes.explanation: Exceptional cutaway joke. The casting of Conan's younger self being dumped by Liz Lemon is already funny, but 'Now I'll never lose it!' as a threat/prophecy about a man who has been very publicly married for decades is a perfect comedic escalation. The self-deprecation implied about Conan's love life is wonderful. Justifies 8.5 for structure and originality.

jokes.text: Jenna: 'I'm afraid to even tell her that I frenched her dad on New Year's.'
jokes.setup: Jenna says Liz will cut people off for doing nothing
jokes.punchline: She then reveals she's afraid to tell Liz she kissed her dad on New Year's — the use of 'frenched' and the casualness of the admission is the joke
jokes.explanation: The word 'frenched' is the right period-specific euphemism — it's both funny and tells us exactly what happened. Jenna's delivery of it as a casual confession in the middle of a concern about Liz's grudges is good.

jokes.text: Jack: 'I spent Christmas alone in the Hamptons, drinking scotch and throwing firecrackers at Billy Joel's dog!'
jokes.setup: Jack is having a vulnerable breakdown about being alone and in a bad place
jokes.punchline: His Christmas activity was throwing firecrackers at Billy Joel's dog — a perfectly specific Hampton-resident grievance
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best character lines. The specificity of Billy Joel's dog as the victim of Jack's depression is inspired — it implies a longstanding neighbor dispute, a class-specific location (Hamptons), and Jack's specific form of misery (not violence to people, but to dogs of piano legends). Justifies 8+ for originality and character integration.

jokes.text: Jack's daughter enters: 'Daddy, please stop crying.'
jokes.setup: Jack has broken down crying in his monologue about loneliness
jokes.punchline: His small daughter enters — 'Daddy, please stop crying' — a perfect button to his breakdown
jokes.explanation: The child's flat request 'please stop crying' as a button to Jack's elaborate breakdown is perfect. The economy is superb — four words that completely deflate the drama.

jokes.text: Lutz reveals he wrote his name for the lunch pick on flypaper — 'I'm five steps ahead of you, you sons of bitches!'
jokes.setup: The lunch group tries to restart the alphabetical pick to override Lutz
jokes.punchline: A new can is produced — and it's full of Lutz's name on flypaper, which sticks to everyone. 'I'm five steps ahead of you, you sons of bitches!'
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's greatest structural comedy achievements. Lutz's long game — writing his name on flypaper in advance — is a perfect escalation of the running lunch gag. 'I'm five steps ahead of you, you sons of bitches!' as his victory cry is the ideal character moment. This is years of comedic setup paying off in one brilliantly petty act. Fully justifies 8.6.

jokes.text: Cerie announces 'technically this is season 8 since the show was canceled two weeks ago'
jokes.setup: The group tries to override Lutz's pick by invoking alphabetical order
jokes.punchline: Cerie points out that since TGS was officially canceled, this episode technically starts a new season — which resets the alphabet
jokes.explanation: Great structural escalation of the lunch gag — Cerie's lawyerly technicality is unexpected from a character usually played as oblivious. The show-within-show meta reference adds another layer.

jokes.text: Lutz has changed his name to 'Aardvark' to be first alphabetically
jokes.setup: The new season resets the alphabet — whoever is first alphabetically picks lunch
jokes.punchline: Lutz has legally (or otherwise) changed his name to 'Aardvark' to be first alphabetically — 'Shh. Shh, shh, shh, shh, shh.'
jokes.explanation: This is the single best joke in the episode and one of the great 30 Rock escalation payoffs. Lutz changing his name to 'Aardvark' to be first alphabetically is a comedic act of pure pettiness elevated to genius. It implies he did this before the episode even began. The 'Shh. Shh, shh, shh, shh, shh.' as his only response to being called insane is perfect. This is a 9+ level joke — it's structurally perfect, entirely character-specific, original, and the payoff of a long running gag. Easily competes with the anchor examples.

jokes.text: The Rural Juror musical: 'The Irma Luhrmer-merman murder / turned the bird's word lurid...' — Jenna performing the title song from her Broadway musical
jokes.setup: Jenna says she's doing a Broadway musical adaptation of 'The Rural Juror'
jokes.punchline: The title song is an extended tongue-twister of Rural Juror rhymes — 'The Irma Luhrmer-merman murder / turned the bird's word lurid...'
jokes.explanation: The Rural Juror is a series-long running gag — the barely-pronounceable title is finally given full musical treatment. The tongue-twisting verse is genuinely well-crafted as a parody of overwrought Broadway lyrics that happen to be phonetically impossible. 'Khari Wuhrer' landing as a rhyme is inspired.

jokes.text: Jenna explains acting technique: 'To act drunk, you just wear two different-sized heels. And to cry, you just clutch a shard of broken glass.'
jokes.setup: Kenneth challenges Jenna to show real emotion, not acting tricks
jokes.punchline: Jenna reveals her acting tricks — different-sized heels for drunk, broken glass for crying — both utterly insane and weirdly specific
jokes.explanation: One of Jenna's best moments. The two-different-sized-heels drunk trick is inspired — it's absurd but actually has a internal logic. The broken glass for crying is both funnier and darker, implying she physically injures herself to access emotions. These are perfectly Jenna: vain, insane, oddly specific. Justifies 8.5.

jokes.text: Jenna: 'Well, that's not gonna be easy, Kenneth, considering I'm the only person who works here.'
jokes.setup: Kenneth suggests Jenna find something or someone she'll miss to access real emotion
jokes.punchline: Jenna insists she's the only person who works at the show — completely erasing everyone else's existence with classic Jenna narcissism
jokes.explanation: Perfect Jenna line — solipsism compressed to maximum. The flat confidence of 'I'm the only person who works here' is quintessential.

jokes.text: Tracy explains how to fake your own death, including the $70 deposit — 'Why would a guy planning to fake his death deposit $70? He wouldn't!'
jokes.setup: Pete mentions Jack is acting crazy — Tracy recognizes the signs of faking one's own death
jokes.punchline: Tracy's detailed knowledge of faking your death includes the $70 deposit gambit — and his detailed logic about why it works is delivered with complete sincerity
jokes.explanation: Tracy's death-faking expertise is hilarious because it's so specific and so earnestly explained. The $70 reverse-psychology is comedic gold — the explanation ('Why would a guy planning to fake his death deposit $70? He wouldn't!') is perfectly circular logic delivered as wisdom.

jokes.text: Jack to Liz: 'Your light always shone the brightest, baby.' — delivered ominously before the 'last' show
jokes.setup: Jack appears to be saying goodbye in the way someone would before a suicide
jokes.punchline: The over-the-top farewell language ('your light always shone the brightest') plays like a suicide note — but delivered to Liz's face
jokes.explanation: The dramatic irony (we suspect what's happening from Tracy's tip) makes this land as dark comedy. Effective setup for the fake death reveal.

jokes.text: Grizz reveals his uncle left him a bed and breakfast outside Santa Fe — 'I'm gonna be a real fish out of water.'
jokes.setup: Liz notices Grizz is distracted and asks what's happening
jokes.punchline: Grizz — a giant intimidating man — is going to run a bed and breakfast. The visual contrast is the joke. 'Fish out of water' is an understatement.
jokes.explanation: Solid character farewell joke — Grizz as a B&B proprietor is a genuinely funny image. The understated 'fish out of water' is correct.

jokes.text: Lutz's speech: 'I was Lutz — dumb, old, uncool, part-Inuit, bisexual, 51-year-old Lutz!'
jokes.setup: Lutz finally confronts the staff about years of mistreatment
jokes.punchline: His self-description — 'part-Inuit, bisexual, 51-year-old Lutz' — is a character revelation delivered as a grievance list
jokes.explanation: The addition of 'part-Inuit, bisexual' as identity details we've never heard before — dumped in Lutz's list of grievances in the finale — is a great 30 Rock move. The complete identity reveal in a tirade is earned and funny.

jokes.text: Lutz: 'And when that sandwich slides out of you in a week, look at it, because that is Lutz's revenge!'
jokes.setup: Lutz declares his final revenge on the lunch group
jokes.punchline: His revenge is Blimpie's — and specifically the digestive aftermath in a week's time. 'That is Lutz's revenge!'
jokes.explanation: The digestive revenge framing is both gross and structurally perfect — Lutz's revenge will continue to haunt them in the most mundane and visceral way possible. 'Lutz's revenge' as a concept is perfect for the show's finale. One of Lutz's all-time great moments.

jokes.text: Lutz's prophecy: 'And when that sandwich slides out of you in a week, look at it, because that is Lutz's revenge!'
jokes.setup: Lutz concludes his revenge manifesto
jokes.punchline: The ultimate revenge is that a Blimpie's sandwich will eventually exit their bodies — and he wants them to contemplate this and know it was him
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's finest moments. 'That is Lutz's revenge' applied to the inevitable digestive outcome of eating Blimpie's is dark, specific, and extraordinarily funny. The long timeline ('in a week') adds to the absurdity — Lutz is planning a revenge that won't be felt for days and requires the victim to pause in contemplation. Extraordinary combination of dark humor, character specificity, and scatological absurdism. Very quotable.

jokes.text: Liz gives Cerie the lunch order — Nobu 57 and Make My Cake in Harlem — then 'I'll be back. I hope.'
jokes.setup: After defeating Lutz, Liz gives Cerie the real lunch order
jokes.punchline: 'I'll be back. I hope.' — said while going to find Tracy in a strip club, acknowledging the real danger of that errand
jokes.explanation: A nice button — 'I hope' acknowledges the genuine peril of strip club negotiations. Competent.

jokes.text: Tracy at the strip club: 'Give it up for Liz Lemon, everybody! The least molested person in here.'
jokes.setup: Liz finds Tracy at a strip club
jokes.punchline: Tracy introduces Liz to the crowd as 'the least molested person in here' — a darkly specific compliment about the strip club clientele
jokes.explanation: 'The least molested person in here' is a perfect Tracy-in-a-strip-club joke — it says everything about the location without saying it directly. The specificity of 'least molested' rather than 'unharmed' implies a spectrum. Strong economy.

jokes.text: Stripper at the strip club (Tracy's hiding place): 'Give it up for Liz Lemon, everybody! The least molested person in here.'
jokes.setup: Liz has tracked Tracy to a strip club — his 'closest thing to a church'
jokes.punchline: The MC announces Liz as 'the least molested person in here'
jokes.explanation: Excellent throwaway joke. 'The least molested person in here' as an MC announcement is both funny and grimly specific — it works as a joke about the environment AND as a Liz Lemon character joke (her chronic unapproachability/awkwardness in any setting). The word 'molested' makes it darker and funnier than a simpler formulation.

jokes.text: Tracy's speech about not knowing how to say goodbye: 'My dad going to get a pack of smokes and never coming back, all those foster parents talking about adopting me and never did.'
jokes.setup: Tracy explains why he's been trying to ruin the show — he doesn't want to say goodbye
jokes.punchline: He lists the goodbyes he's experienced — father leaving for cigarettes (the classic abandonment joke), foster parents who never adopted — delivered with complete sincerity that makes it funnier
jokes.explanation: Tracy's trauma as comedy — the cigarette abandonment is a known comedic shorthand but Tracy's specific delivery makes it feel character-authentic. The emotional core is real, which makes it funnier.

jokes.text: Liz's honest goodbye to Tracy: 'We're probably not gonna hang out after this... You'll say you're gonna invite me to your house and it's never gonna happen. And I'll see on TV that it's your birthday and I'll forget to call.'
jokes.setup: Tracy asks for a 'hard-core truth goodbye'
jokes.punchline: Liz delivers a brutally honest assessment of how their relationship will actually end — no drama, just natural drift, forgotten birthdays, uninvited house visits
jokes.explanation: This is both the episode's most emotionally honest moment and one of its best comedic constructions. The brutal specificity of 'I'll see on TV that it's your birthday and I'll forget to call' is devastating and true. The joke works because it's painfully accurate to how most real work-friendships end. The comedy is in the delivery and the honesty.

jokes.text: Tracy's response: 'Brutally honest... I like that.'
jokes.setup: Liz has delivered a genuinely bleak honest goodbye
jokes.punchline: Tracy's sincere appreciation of the brutal honesty — he finds it refreshing, not sad
jokes.explanation: Works as a small punctuation joke — Tracy's response is perfectly in character and the comedic beat is necessary to signal we're still in comedy mode after the genuine emotion.

jokes.text: Tracy: 'Brutally honest. I like that.' — then goes back to watch a 'skank train' before the show
jokes.setup: Liz delivers her sincere brutal goodbye
jokes.punchline: Tracy appreciates it — 'Brutally honest. I like that.' — then says he'll come back but they need to watch 'this first' as strippers continue performing
jokes.explanation: Good button — the emotional moment is immediately undercut by Tracy's need to watch the performance. 'Ride the train, ladies' as the callback line is perfectly Tracy.

jokes.text: The Lutz/Blimpie finale: food arrives but it's cupcake sandwiches from Cerie's order; writers celebrate, then Lutz runs in covered in Blimpie's food — the writers scatter screaming 'Cover the food!'
jokes.setup: The food from Cerie's order has arrived — the Blimpie's conflict appears to be resolved
jokes.punchline: Lutz arrives with actual Blimpie's food (implied he's brought it/thrown it) and chaos ensues
jokes.explanation: Good physical comedy escalation of the Blimpie gag. The shift from triumph (cupcake sandwiches!) to panic ('Cover the food!') is a classic farce beat. Lutz's commitment to Blimpie's as his revenge weapon, even now, is the running gag's physical climax.

jokes.text: Jack's fake video suicide note: 'Try not to blame yourself. How were you to know I was in such a dark place that the smallest thing — for example, a close friend's refusal to reconcile — would be the final straw.'
jokes.setup: Liz finds Jack's phone and discovers a video labeled 'suicide note'
jokes.punchline: The 'suicide note' video immediately blames Liz — 'a close friend's refusal to reconcile' — making it transparently a guilt trip disguised as a farewell
jokes.explanation: The 'suicide note as passive-aggressive guilt trip' structure is very Jack Donaghy. The formal video format adds absurdity. 'The smallest thing — for example' is perfectly manipulative.

jokes.text: Jack's parting gift: 'Go to YouTube and search Hamlet the mini pig goes downstairs.' Liz: '...No! Phone first! I'll watch the pig video in the cab.'
jokes.setup: Jack's video suicide note promises a 'parting gift'
jokes.punchline: The gift is a YouTube video of a mini pig named Hamlet going downstairs. Liz's reaction — almost watching it immediately before correcting herself — is the joke.
jokes.explanation: The pig video is perfectly chosen as the one thing that could distract Liz from a crisis. 'I'll watch the pig video in the cab' as a self-compromise is a great Liz Lemon moment. 'Hamlet' as the pig's name adds a literary layer.

jokes.text: Tracy's final goodbye to the cast: 'Guys, to be honest, you are nerds, and one of you is very funny. Good-bye forever.'
jokes.setup: Tracy says final goodbyes to the TGS staff
jokes.punchline: 'You are nerds, and one of you is very funny' — a perfectly backhanded compliment, leaving 'which one?' as the hanging question. 'Good-bye forever.'
jokes.explanation: One of Tracy's best final-season lines. 'One of you is very funny' is a perfect Tracy backhanded compliment — the ambiguity about who is devastating and funny. Brilliant economy. The 'Good-bye forever' button is exactly right.

jokes.text: Tracy to Pete: 'Good-bye, Petey Pete. I will forget you.' Pete: 'I sure hope so, tray. I sure hope so.'
jokes.setup: Tracy delivers individual goodbyes
jokes.punchline: Tracy promises to forget Pete; Pete's response — 'I sure hope so, Tray. I sure hope so.' — reveals Pete's desire to be forgotten (and the relief of escape)
jokes.explanation: Pete's 'I sure hope so' is the perfect button — it's genuinely moving and funny simultaneously. Pete's relief at being forgotten by Tracy is a perfect encapsulation of their seven-year relationship.

jokes.text: Tracy to Liz: 'My Bologna, in all honesty — I'm going out for cigarettes now. And I'll be home in 15 minutes.'
jokes.setup: After the brutally honest goodbye, Tracy says his final farewell to Liz before the show
jokes.punchline: He uses the 'going out for cigarettes' line — which he earlier acknowledged as the classic abandonment trope — but promises 15 minutes. It's both a callback and a sincere promise.
jokes.explanation: This is a masterful callback. Tracy earlier described his abandonment trauma using the 'going out for cigarettes' metaphor. Here he inverts it — he IS going out for cigarettes, but he specifies 'and I'll be home in 15 minutes.' He's breaking the cycle. It's both funny and genuinely moving. One of the episode's emotional peaks. Justifies 8.8.

jokes.text: Liz sprinting to find Jack: 'Don't you want to know how Mad Men ends? Oh, Don goes to work for Peggy!'
jokes.setup: Liz finds Jack apparently about to fake his death/leave and screams to stop him
jokes.punchline: Her incentive to stop him is spoiling Mad Men's ending — then immediately spoiling it anyway: 'Oh, Don goes to work for Peggy!'
jokes.explanation: One of the most quoted moments in the episode. The fake Mad Men spoiler (which the show aired before Mad Men ended) is simultaneously meta, funny, and a perfect Liz move — she blurts it out as a threat then immediately delivers it. 'Don goes to work for Peggy' as a deliberately underwhelming fake ending is inspired.

jokes.text: Jack: 'I have to find my bliss, which, for once, is not an acronym for Beautiful Ladies In Short Shorts.'
jokes.setup: Jack says he needs to find his bliss
jokes.punchline: He clarifies that 'bliss' is not an acronym for 'Beautiful Ladies In Short Shorts' — implying this is a real acronym he has used before
jokes.explanation: 'For once' is the key word — it implies a documented history of Jack using 'BLISS' as an acronym for something lewd. The specificity of 'Beautiful Ladies In Short Shorts' as the prior usage is perfectly Jack. Great economy.

jokes.text: Jack's elaborate etymology of 'love' — 'Old High German luba, from Latin lubere, meaning to be pleasing, as used by Anglo-Saxon forefathers in reference to a hot bowl of bear meat or your enemy's skull... Split.' — to avoid saying 'I love you'
jokes.setup: Jack wants to express his feelings for Liz without using the word 'love' in a romantic context
jokes.punchline: He delivers a full etymological lecture on the word's history to defuse any romantic implication — ending with 'a hot bowl of bear meat or your enemy's skull... Split.'
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's finest Jack Donaghy moments and a perfect series finale joke. The elaborate linguistic armor he deploys to say 'I love you' is quintessentially Jack — the man who cannot be vulnerable, so instead weaponizes scholarship. 'Your enemy's skull... Split.' as the preferred analogy over romance is perfect. The word 'split' after the pause is a great comedic button. Justifies 8.6.

jokes.text: Jack's circumlocution for 'I love you': etymology of 'luba' from Old High German, through Latin 'lubere,' explained as analogous to 'a hot bowl of bear meat or your enemy's skull... split.'
jokes.setup: Jack wants to tell Liz something but won't use the word 'love' for fear it implies romance
jokes.punchline: He delivers a full academic etymological justification for using the word 'love' platonically, framing their relationship as equivalent to 'a hot bowl of bear meat or your enemy's skull, split'
jokes.explanation: The episode's finest sustained joke and arguably among 30 Rock's best series-finale moments. Jack's inability to say 'I love you' without a 50-word etymological defense that frames the relationship as equivalent to bear meat and a split enemy skull is perfectly constructed: it's funny, it's in-character, it's emotionally resonant, and the Anglo-Saxon framing is an absurdist masterstroke. The punchline — Liz simply saying 'I love you too, Jack' — is the correct comedic deflation of all his effort. Very high craft scores are entirely justified. One of the best comedy exchanges of the entire series.

jokes.text: 'Thank you, America. That's our show. Not a lot of people watched it. But the joke's on you, 'cause we got paid anyway.'
jokes.setup: Liz signs off on the final TGS episode
jokes.punchline: The sign-off acknowledges that TGS (and by meta-extension, 30 Rock) wasn't widely watched — 'not a lot of people watched it. But the joke's on you, 'cause we got paid anyway.'
jokes.explanation: A perfect meta series-finale joke. 30 Rock famously had critical acclaim but low ratings — this joke directly addresses that, with the cast getting paid regardless. The defiant 'but the joke's on you' is perfect. One of the episode's most quotable and self-aware moments.

jokes.text: Jack's big insight from his boat trip: 'Clear dishwashers! So you can see what's going on inside it!' — delivered as a revelation
jokes.setup: Jack says he'll be a new man after months on his boat — then turns around immediately
jokes.punchline: He's been on the boat for roughly three minutes and already has his 'insight': see-through dishwashers. Both he and Liz react with complete genuine enthusiasm.
jokes.explanation: Exceptional series finale joke. The build — Jack's profound farewell, sailing away, 'the next time you see me I'll be a new man' — makes the immediate turn even funnier. 'Clear dishwashers!' is both a completely absurd non-revelation and genuinely a good idea, which is what makes it perfect. Both characters being fully enthusiastic about this is the ideal button. One of the episode's top moments.

jokes.text: Pete is found by his wife Paula in the parking lot — she calls him 'Sam' — he tries to claim amnesia but breaks immediately: 'I practiced this!'
jokes.setup: Pete has apparently been trying to fake his own identity to escape Paula
jokes.punchline: She calls him 'Sam'; he tries amnesia; immediately breaks — 'Oh, damn it! I practiced this!'
jokes.explanation: 'Oh, damn it! I practiced this!' reveals that Pete planned and rehearsed his fake identity, which makes it much funnier. The immediate failure of a prepared deception is a great structural beat. Very Pete.

jokes.text: Tracy's credits speech: 'I want to thank the brilliant Kevin Grisham, the amazing John Stamos, the incomparable Judge Judy Scheindlin.' — then steals the credits from another actor
jokes.setup: End credits roll and someone is listing acknowledgments
jokes.punchline: Tracy credits completely fictional names alongside Judge Judy, then physically shoves another actor aside to steal their credit mention — 'See ya later, suckers! Meep-meep! Pyung!'
jokes.explanation: Judge Judy alongside Kevin Grisham in a sincere thank-you is a perfect list. The physical steal of the credits spot is visually funny. 'Meep-meep! Pyung!' as an exit is peak Tracy.

jokes.text: Tracy calls Liz to tell her 'my dad finally came back from getting cigarettes' — the cigarette running gag resolved
jokes.setup: The cigarette abandonment motif has been used throughout the episode
jokes.punchline: Post-finale, Tracy calls Liz to say his dad came back from getting cigarettes — the childhood trauma resolved with a throwaway phone call
jokes.explanation: One of the greatest callbacks in 30 Rock history and arguably the episode's most emotionally complete joke. The cigarette abandonment joke — set up in Tracy's speech, subverted in his goodbye to Liz, and now paid off years later — is resolved in a single line. The economy is perfect. The implication that his dad coming back is just a casual piece of news Tracy mentions between other calls is both funny and deeply affecting. Tied with Lutz-Aardvark for the episode's highest craft score.

jokes.text: Jack calls Liz from the boat: 'Don't forget Tracy's birthday.'
jokes.setup: The honest goodbye speech included 'I'll see on TV that it's your birthday and forget to call'
jokes.punchline: Jack immediately calls after departure to remind Liz about Tracy's birthday — suggesting he too doesn't want to be the person who forgets
jokes.explanation: Perfect callback — Jack's immediate call to remind Liz about Tracy's birthday proves he was listening and cares about the small things. The economy is superb. A beautiful button on the honest-goodbye speech.

jokes.text: New assistant is named Sam — Jack: 'Wait, you're Sam?' — mirroring the Pete/Paula 'Sam' scene
jokes.setup: Jack is introduced to his new second assistant
jokes.punchline: The new assistant is named Sam — echoing Pete's fake identity — and the show ends implying a new cycle beginning
jokes.explanation: The 'Sam' callback is nice but softer than the other finale callbacks. Works as a structural echo and suggests cyclical continuation.

jokes.text: The show-within-a-show flash-forward: TGS is now a period piece set at '30 Rockefeller Plaza' — based on stories 'my great-grandmother told me'
jokes.setup: A flash-forward shows a future TV executive pitching or watching a show
jokes.punchline: The show being watched IS 30 Rock — now a historical period piece based on 'stories my great-grandmother told me' — revealing we've been watching a show-within-a-show all along
jokes.explanation: The series' ultimate meta joke — 30 Rock ends by revealing it was always a show-within-a-show, now presented as a period piece. 'Stories my great-grandmother told me' implies Liz's descendants made 30 Rock into TGS, which was always based on Liz's life. The structural recursion is genuinely inventive. This is series-finale-level meta-comedy that requires the full seven seasons to land. Justifies the high score.

tmdb_overview: Jenna prepares an emotional farewell song as the cast and crew reunite for one final "TGS".
insight: Series finale delivers 105 jokes at 2.02-per-minute clip for elite 90.6 score.
